_comment: Culture regions - the tier above traditions.
The site reports '181 Traditions' and lists them flat. The entity data actually
holds 270 distinct `mythology` values, 142 of which have three entities or fewer,
so most of that list is a dead end. Worse, several are not traditions at all:
`weapons`, `armor`, `underworlds` and `mystical` are category words that leaked
into the field, and `german american` sits beside `german-american`.
Grouping the real traditions into regions gives a reader ten doors instead of a
hundred and eighty, and gives the long tail somewhere to live other than the
`members` are matched case-insensitively against the `mythology` field, with
hyphens, underscores and spaces treated as the same character - which is what
`notTraditions` are values excluded from the tradition tier entirely. They are
not deleted: the entities carrying them keep their pages, and the values are
reported by the build so the underlying data can be repaired.

regions.name: Classical Mediterranean
regions.blurb: Greece and Rome, and the Etruscans they borrowed from - the best-documented pantheons in the collection, and the template most Western readers measure the others against.

regions.name: Norse & Germanic
regions.blurb: The northern pantheon and its cousins - a mythology preserved largely by people writing it down after they had stopped believing it.

regions.name: Celtic & Insular
regions.blurb: Ireland, Wales, Scotland and Brittany, plus the Arthurian material that grew out of them and outgrew them.

regions.name: Ancient Near East
regions.blurb: Sumer, Babylon, Assyria, Canaan and Persia - the oldest written myths anywhere, and the source of flood and creation stories that travelled a long way.

regions.name: Egypt & the Nile
regions.blurb: Three thousand years of a single tradition, unusually concerned with what happens after death and unusually specific about it.

regions.name: Abrahamic Traditions
regions.blurb: Jewish, Christian and Islamic material - scripture, apocrypha, and the angels and demons that accumulated around them.

regions.name: South Asia
regions.blurb: Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions - the largest living mythologies here, still in daily practice rather than only in texts.

regions.name: East Asia
regions.blurb: China, Japan and Korea - three traditions that borrowed from each other continuously and stayed distinct.

regions.name: Southeast Asia & the Pacific
regions.blurb: Island traditions across an ocean - Polynesian voyaging myth, Aboriginal Dreaming, and the archipelago cultures between them.

regions.name: Africa
regions.blurb: Yoruba, Akan, Zulu and the diaspora traditions carried to the Americas - among the most under-recorded material in the collection.

regions.name: The Americas
regions.blurb: Aztec, Maya and Inca, and the many North American nations - traditions that survived deliberate attempts to erase them.

regions.name: Northern & Eastern Europe
regions.blurb: Slavic, Baltic and Finno-Ugric traditions - forest mythologies, recorded late and often only in folk song.

regions.name: Western Europe
regions.blurb: French, Iberian and Alpine folklore - the local traditions that persisted under Christianity rather than being replaced by it.

regions.name: Esoteric & Occult
regions.blurb: Tarot, alchemy, hermeticism and the Western magical tradition - systems that borrowed gods from everywhere and rearranged them.
